technique: withholding — what the poem refuses to name or explain, and why that works
lesson: Today we work on one technique. It's called withholding. That means the poem leaves something out on purpose and never names it directly. Look at what this poem won't tell you. It says "the long list that only shortens by the hand." It never tells you what's on that list. It says "There's good work with your name on it," but it never says what the work is. It says "what the day asks," and leaves the asking blank. It works because your mind fills the gap with your own tasks. When the poem won't name the work, you supply it, so the poem ends up being about your day, not the speaker's. Try this: write about a duty you have, but never say what the duty is—describe only getting ready to do it. The second time through, listen for every place the poem points at something and refuses to name it. Here is the poem.
poem:
A crow drops out of the bare oak crown,
lands heavy on the frost-stiff field, and walks
the furrows it has learned by heart, tilting
one eye down, then the other, methodical,
turning each cold clod to see what's under it.
It does not hurry. It takes what the ground will give
and lets the rest go, lifts off when it's done.
Over the hill the gray comes up unhurried,
the same hour it always was, no fuss in it.
You stand in the doorway counting what the day asks,
the long list that only shortens by the hand—
and the hand is yours, and it is willing.

There's good work with your name on it—
rise and go put your hands to it.
